title: 1.1–1.3 Catch-Up
contentObjective: I can show I am caught up on Lessons 1.1–1.3 by using each lesson's big idea in mixed practice.
languageObjective: I can explain which lesson's big idea I used and how, using key vocabulary from Lessons 1.1–1.3.

vocabulary.definition: Anyone who uses mathematical thinking — which is everyone, every day.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cualquiera que use el pensamiento matemático, es decir, todos, todos los días.
vocabulary.example: Splitting a bill, packing a bag, keeping score.
vocabulary.visual: Splitting a bill 4 ways at dinner — that is a doer of math.
vocabulary.cloze: Anyone who uses mathematical thinking is a ___ ___ ___.

examples.text: Working out you need to leave at 7:40 to catch the 7:55 bus
examples.why: You used numbers and reasoning to make a decision.

examples.text: Only people who finish a worksheet first
examples.why: Speed is not what makes someone a doer of math.

vocabulary.definition: Your own history with mathematics — what you have done, felt, and learned so far.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Tu propia historia con las matemáticas: lo que has hecho, sentido y aprendido.
vocabulary.example: “I liked math until fractions, and now I like it again.”
vocabulary.visual: “In 3rd grade I hated fractions; this year I can explain them.”
vocabulary.cloze: Your history with mathematics — what you have done and felt — is your ___ ___.

examples.text: “Math felt scary until I learned to draw the problem.”
examples.why: It describes how your thinking changed over time.

examples.text: “I got an 85 on the last test.”
examples.why: One score is a moment, not the story of your thinking.

vocabulary.definition: Something you already do well and can share with others.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Algo que ya haces bien y puedes compartir con otros.
vocabulary.visual: “I am good at mental math with money” — a strength you can teach.
vocabulary.cloze: Something you already do well and can share with others is a ___.

examples.text: Explaining your steps so a partner can follow them
examples.why: It is something you do well that helps the group.

examples.text: Something you are still learning to do
examples.why: That is a goal, not yet a strength.

vocabulary.definition: To break a number into parts that add, subtract, multiply, or divide back to it.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Separar un número en partes que se combinan para volver a formarlo.
vocabulary.visual: 78.5 = 70 + 8.5, and also 157 ÷ 2 — both rebuild the same number.
vocabulary.cloze: To break a number into parts that rebuild it exactly is to ___ it.

examples.why: The parts add back to exactly the original number.
The parts do not rebuild the number — 0.76 went missing.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful, without counting every one.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una respuesta razonada, lo bastante cercana para ser útil, sin contar todo.
vocabulary.example: About how many people fit on the Ferris wheel?
vocabulary.visual: 20 cars × about 4 riders ≈ 80 people on the Ferris wheel.
vocabulary.cloze: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful is an ___.

examples.text: “About 80 riders” when the true count is 78
examples.why: Close enough to plan with, and it took no counting.

examples.text: Any number you say without thinking
examples.why: An estimate is reasoned, not random.

vocabulary.definition: An amount in a problem — a number with a meaning attached, like 540 meters.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una cantidad en un problema: un número con un significado, como 540 metros.
vocabulary.example: The heights of the buildings are the quantities in the problem.
vocabulary.visual: 540 meters — the number 540 AND what it measures.
vocabulary.cloze: A number with a meaning attached, like 540 meters, is a ___.

examples.why: A number together with what it counts.
Without a unit or a meaning it is only a number.

vocabulary.definition: How two quantities compare or connect to each other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cómo se comparan o se conectan dos cantidades entre sí.
vocabulary.example: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel.
vocabulary.visual: 1 hour → 48 km, 2 hours → 96 km: as one grows, so does the other.
vocabulary.cloze: How two quantities connect or change together is a ___.

examples.why: One quantity responds when the other changes.

examples.text: A student's height and their house number
examples.why: Neither one moves because of the other.

vocabulary.definition: A plan for how to solve a problem before you start computing.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un plan para resolver un problema antes de empezar a calcular.
vocabulary.example: We can think about how the quantities in the problem relate.
vocabulary.visual: “I will draw a tape diagram first, then divide” — chosen before computing.
vocabulary.cloze: The plan you choose before you start computing is your ___.

examples.text: Deciding to count one small group of peas first
examples.why: It is a plan you choose before you compute.
That is the result. A strategy is the plan that gets you there.

vocabulary.definition: A picture, diagram, table, or equation that shows the mathematics in a situation.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un dibujo, diagrama, tabla o ecuación que muestra las matemáticas de una situación.
vocabulary.example: A tape diagram representing 4,000 passengers split into tram rides.
vocabulary.visual: The same 12 shown three ways: a tape diagram, a table, and 3 × 4.
vocabulary.cloze: A drawing, table, or equation that shows the math in a situation is a ___.

examples.text: A table pairing rides with minutes
examples.why: It shows the mathematics of the situation in an organized form.

examples.text: A drawing of the tram because it looks nice
examples.why: A picture that carries no quantities shows no mathematics.

vocabulary.definition: A rectangle cut into equal parts that helps you visualize how a total breaks apart.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un rectángulo dividido en partes iguales que te ayuda a visualizar cómo se separa un total.
vocabulary.example: A bar for 4,000 passengers cut into equal groups of 80.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 1.1–1.3: 1.1 Math is Mine, 1.2 Math is Exploring and Thinking, 1.3 Math is In My World. Work one example from each lesson, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: Catch-Up — Lessons 1.1–1.3
conceptIntro.intro: Catch up on Lessons 1.1–1.3: one worked example and one quick check for each lesson.
conceptIntro.introEs: Ponte al día con las Lecciones 1.1 a 1.3: un ejemplo resuelto y una comprobación rápida por lección.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 1.1: To estimate, find equal groups and multiply easy numbers, and to decompose, break a number into parts that rebuild it exactly. • 1.2: Make sense of the problem first, then plan: count a small group you can see and multiply to estimate the whole. • 1.3: A tape diagram shows why we divide, and a table shows how the totals grow, so the right tool makes the math clear.
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: 1.1: Para estimar, busca grupos iguales y multiplica números fáciles, y para descomponer, separa un número en partes que lo vuelven a formar exactamente. • 1.2: Primero entiende el problema y luego planea: cuenta un grupo pequeño que puedas ver y multiplica para estimar el total. • 1.3: Un diagrama de barras muestra por qué dividimos, y una tabla muestra cómo crecen los totales, así que la herramienta correcta aclara las matemáticas.

lines: A Ferris wheel has 20 cars. About 4 people fit in each car. About how many people can ride at one time?
Estimate the size of one group: about 4 people
Multiply the groups by the group size: 20 × 4 = 80
About 80 people can ride at one time.
One small group of peas has about 10 peas. About 12 groups like it fill the bowl. About how many peas are in the bowl?
Count one small group: about 10 peas
Count how many groups fill the bowl: about 12 groups
Multiply the groups by the group size: 12 × 10 = 120
About 120 peas are in the bowl.
One tram ride takes 12.5 minutes. How many minutes do 50 rides take?

Multiplica los grupos por el tamaño de cada grupo: 20 × 4 = 80

Cuenta cuántos grupos llenan el tazón: alrededor de 12 grupos

Hay unos 120 chícharos en el tazón.

Multiplica por 5 para llegar a 50 viajes: 125 × 5 = 625

connect.scenario: It takes 35 minutes for one tram car to make the 5-mile round trip, from valley to mountain top and back down — including time for passengers to disembark and embark at each station. You want to know how many round trips a single tram car completes in 10 hours.
connect.promptQuestion: What tool can you use to represent the relationship between time and round trips, and how does it answer the question?
connect.prompt: Name the tool you would use to show the relationship — a ___ of values — then name the two quantities in the problem: ___ and ___ .

check.stem: The tram problem asks how many round trips fit in 10 hours. What is the FIRST thing you must find before you can read the answer off your table?
choices: How many miles the tram travels in total
How many passengers ride each trip
How many minutes are in 10 hours, so the units match the table
check.explanation: The table is built in minutes, but the question gives hours. Convert first: 10 hours = 600 minutes. Now you can find where 600 falls among the table's rows.
check.stemEs: El problema del teleférico pregunta cuántos viajes redondos caben en 10 horas. ¿Qué es lo primero que debes hallar antes de poder leer la respuesta en tu tabla?
check.explanationEs: La tabla está armada en minutos, pero la pregunta da horas. Convierte primero: 10 horas = 600 minutos. Ahora puedes hallar dónde cae el 600 entre las filas de la tabla.
choicesEs: Cuántas millas recorre el teleférico en total
Cuántos pasajeros viajan en cada viaje
Cuántos minutos hay en 10 horas, para que las unidades coincidan con la tabla

check.stem: Using the table (35→1, 175→5, 350→10, 525→15, 700→20 minutes→trips), why does the answer end up being 17 round trips, not 18?
choices: 18 trips is closer to 600 minutes, so it is the better estimate
17 trips take 595 minutes, which fits within 600, but an 18th trip would need 630 minutes, past the limit
A round trip can be counted as complete even if it is only partly finished
The table only lists rows up to 20, so 17 is the safe middle choice
check.explanation: Try 17 trips: 17 × 35 = 595 minutes. That is still inside the 600-minute limit. Try 18: 18 × 35 = 630 minutes, which goes past it. A round trip only counts once it is fully complete.
check.stemEs: Usando la tabla (35→1, 175→5, 350→10, 525→15, 700→20 minutos→viajes), ¿por qué la respuesta termina siendo 17 viajes redondos y no 18?
check.explanationEs: Prueba con 17 viajes: 17 × 35 = 595 minutos. Eso todavía está dentro del límite de 600 minutos. Prueba con 18: 18 × 35 = 630 minutos, que se pasa. Un viaje redondo solo cuenta cuando está completo.
choicesEs: 18 viajes queda más cerca de 600 minutos, así que es la mejor estimación
17 viajes toman 595 minutos, que cabe en 600, pero un viaje 18 necesitaría 630 minutos, pasándose del límite
Un viaje redondo se puede contar como completo aunque solo esté terminado a medias
La tabla solo enlista filas hasta 20, así que 17 es la opción segura de en medio

check.stem: 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.14. Why is it risky to round this quotient down to 17 WITHOUT also checking the table?
choices: Rounding down happens to work here, but only the table confirms 17 × 35 stays under 600 while 18 × 35 does not
Rounding down never works for time problems
17.14 should round up to 18 because .14 rounds upward
The table and division always disagree with each other
check.explanation: 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.14. The .14 left over is an unfinished trip, not extra completed ones. Rounding alone does not prove that. Checking the table's real minute totals is what shows 17 is right.
check.stemEs: 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.14. ¿Por qué es riesgoso redondear este cociente a 17 sin revisar también la tabla?
check.explanationEs: 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.14. El .14 que sobra es un viaje sin terminar, no viajes completos de más. Redondear por sí solo no lo prueba. Revisar los totales reales de minutos de la tabla es lo que muestra que 17 es correcto.
choicesEs: Redondear hacia abajo resulta que funciona aquí, pero solo la tabla confirma que 17 × 35 se queda debajo de 600 mientras que 18 × 35 no
Redondear hacia abajo nunca funciona en problemas de tiempo
17.14 debería redondearse a 18 porque .14 redondea hacia arriba
La tabla y la división siempre se contradicen

connect.modelAnswer: The two quantities are the time and the number of round trips. I would build a table of values: 35 minutes for 1 trip, 175 for 5, 350 for 10, 525 for 15, 700 for 20. Ten hours is 600 minutes, which lands between 525 and 700 on my table. Since 17 trips take 595 minutes and an 18th trip would pass 600, a tram car completes 17 round trips in 10 hours. I could also plot the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane and read the answer there.
connect.promptEs: Nombra la herramienta que usarías para mostrar la relación — una ___ de valores — y luego nombra las dos cantidades del problema: ___ y ___ .
connect.scenarioEs: Una cabina de teleférico tarda 35 minutos en hacer el viaje redondo de 5 millas, del valle a la cima de la montaña y de regreso — incluyendo el tiempo para que los pasajeros bajen y suban en cada estación. Quieres saber cuántos viajes redondos completa una sola cabina en 10 horas.
connect.promptQuestionEs: ¿Qué herramienta puedes usar para representar la relación entre el tiempo y los viajes redondos, y cómo responde la pregunta?
connect.modelAnswerEs: Las dos cantidades son el tiempo y el número de viajes redondos. Yo armaría una tabla de valores: 35 minutos para 1 viaje, 175 para 5, 350 para 10, 525 para 15, 700 para 20. Diez horas son 600 minutos, que cae entre 525 y 700 en mi tabla. Como 17 viajes toman 595 minutos y un viaje 18 se pasaría de 600, una cabina completa 17 viajes redondos en 10 horas. También podría marcar los pares ordenados en un plano de coordenadas y leer la respuesta ahí.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.1) About how many people can ride the Ferris wheel at one time if it has 20 cars that each hold about 4 people?
approaching.explanation: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4, which is about 80 people.
choiceFeedback: That divides 20 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 20 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies as if each car held 20 people.
hints: How many groups are there, and how big is each group?
20 groups of 4.
Multiply 20 × 4.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Aproximadamente cuántas personas pueden subir a la rueda de la fortuna a la vez si tiene 20 cabinas y cada una lleva unas 4 personas?
approaching.explanationEs: 20 carros con unos 4 pasajeros cada uno es 20 × 4, que son unas 80 personas.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos grupos hay, y de qué tamaño es cada grupo?
20 grupos de 4.
Multiplica 20 × 4.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.1) Which of these is a correct way to decompose 78.5?
approaching.explanation: 70 + 8.5 = 78.5. Decomposing means the parts must add back to the original number.
hints: Add each option and see what you get.
The parts must total 78.5 exactly.
Add the two parts in each choice. Which total lands exactly on 78.5?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es una manera correcta de descomponer 78.5?
approaching.explanationEs: 70 + 8.5 = 78.5. Descomponer significa que las partes deben sumar de nuevo el número original.
hintsEs: Suma cada opción y mira qué obtienes.
Las partes deben sumar exactamente 78.5.
Suma las dos partes de cada opción. ¿Cuál total cae exactamente en 78.5?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.2) Which of these is a correct way to decompose 105.76?
approaching.explanation: 100 + 5.76 = 105.76. Decomposing means the parts must rebuild the original number exactly.
choiceFeedback: 10 + 5.76 = 15.76 — that drops the hundreds digit of 105.76.
100 + 5.076 = 105.076 — that pushes the digits one decimal place too far right.
105 + 7.6 = 112.6, not 105.76 — the 7 and 6 belong in the tenths and hundredths places.
hints: Add each option and compare to 105.76.
The parts must total 105.76 exactly.
Add the two parts in each choice. Only one total lands exactly on 105.76.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es una manera correcta de descomponer 105.76?
approaching.explanationEs: 100 + 5.76 = 105.76. Descomponer significa que las partes deben reconstruir el número original exactamente.
hintsEs: Suma cada opción y compara con 105.76.
Las partes deben sumar exactamente 105.76.
Suma las dos partes de cada opción. Solo un total cae exactamente en 105.76.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.2) Which is another correct decomposition of 105.76?
approaching.explanation: 110 − 4.24 = 105.76. A decomposition can use subtraction, not only addition.
choiceFeedback: 106 − 0.34 = 105.66 — the difference from 106 is 0.24, not 0.34.
110 − 5.24 = 104.76 — that takes away one whole too many.
110 + 4.24 = 114.24 — that moves away from 105.76 instead of down to it.
hints: Start at 110. How far down is 105.76?
So subtracting 4.24 from 110 works.
approaching.explanationEs: 110 − 4.24 = 105.76. Una descomposición puede usar resta, no solo suma.
hintsEs: Empieza en 110. ¿Qué tanto hay que bajar hasta 105.76?
Así que restar 4.24 de 110 funciona.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.3) One tram ride takes 12.5 minutes. How many minutes do 10 rides take?
approaching.explanation: 12.5 × 10 = 125. Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place to the left.
choiceFeedback: 1.25 moves the decimal point the wrong way — that DIVIDES 12.5 by 10.
22.5 ADDS 12.5 + 10 instead of multiplying.
1,250 multiplies by 100 instead of 10.
hints: You need 10 equal groups of 12.5.
Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point one place.
Which direction makes the number bigger?
approaching.stemEs: Un viaje en tranvía toma 12.5 minutos. ¿Cuántos minutos toman 10 viajes?
approaching.explanationEs: 12.5 × 10 = 125. Multiplicar por 10 mueve cada dígito un lugar a la izquierda.
hintsEs: Necesitas 10 grupos iguales de 12.5.
Multiplicar por 10 mueve el punto decimal un lugar.
¿Qué dirección hace el número más grande?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.3) Five Breaks: which of these is a correct way to decompose 12.5?
approaching.explanation: 10 + 2.5 = 12.5. The parts of a decomposition must rebuild the number exactly.
choiceFeedback: 1 + 2.5 = 3.5 — that drops the tens digit of 12.5.
10 + 2.05 = 12.05 — the 5 slid from the tenths place to the hundredths place.
12 + 5 = 17 — the 5 in 12.5 is five TENTHS, not five ones.
hints: Add each option and compare to 12.5.
What does the 5 in 12.5 stand for?
Add the two parts in each choice, and keep the tenths in mind — 12.5 is 12 and five tenths.
approaching.stemEs: Cinco descomposiciones: ¿cuál de estas es una manera correcta de descomponer 12.5?
approaching.explanationEs: 10 + 2.5 = 12.5. Las partes de una descomposición deben reconstruir el número exactamente.
hintsEs: Suma cada opción y compara con 12.5.
¿Qué representa el 5 de 12.5?
Suma las dos partes de cada opción y ten en cuenta los décimos — 12.5 es 12 y cinco décimos.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.1) Which decomposition of 78.5 uses multiplication correctly?
onLevel.explanation: 39.25 × 2 = 78.5, so halving and doubling is another way to break the number apart.
choiceFeedback: 39 × 2 = 78, which is close but not 78.5.
78.5 × 2 = 157, which doubles the number instead of rebuilding it.
hints: What is half of 78.5?
Half of 78.5 is 39.25.
Two of those halves rebuild it.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál descomposición de 78.5 usa la multiplicación correctamente?
onLevel.explanationEs: 39.25 × 2 = 78.5, así que sacar la mitad y duplicar es otra manera de descomponer el número.
hintsEs: ¿Cuánto es la mitad de 78.5?
La mitad de 78.5 es 39.25.
Dos de esas mitades lo reconstruyen.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.1) A Ferris wheel holds about 78 riders per turn and makes 6 turns an hour. About how many riders per hour?
onLevel.explanation: 78 riders on each of 6 turns is 78 × 6 = 468 riders in an hour.
choiceFeedback: That divides 78 by 6 instead of multiplying.
That adds 78 + 6 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies by 10 instead of 6.
hints: Each turn carries a full load. How many turns?
6 turns of 78 riders.
onLevel.stemEs: Una rueda de la fortuna lleva unos 78 pasajeros por vuelta y da 6 vueltas por hora. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos pasajeros por hora?
onLevel.explanationEs: 78 pasajeros en cada una de 6 vueltas es 78 × 6 = 468 pasajeros en una hora.
hintsEs: Cada vuelta lleva una carga completa. ¿Cuántas vueltas?
6 vueltas de 78 pasajeros.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.2) The Rio de Janeiro building will be 9/10 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
onLevel.explanation: 9/10 × 540: one tenth of 540 is 54, and 9 tenths is 9 × 54 = 486 meters.
choiceFeedback: 54 meters is only 1/10 of 540 — you still need 9 of those tenths.
594 meters ADDS one tenth (540 + 54) instead of taking 9 tenths of 540.
4,860 meters multiplies 540 by 9 but never divides by 10.
hints: First find one tenth of 540.
Multiply that tenth by 9.
onLevel.stemEs: El edificio de Río de Janeiro será 9/10 de alto que el One World Trade Center (540 metros). ¿Qué altura tendrá?
onLevel.explanationEs: 9/10 × 540: un décimo de 540 es 54, y 9 décimos son 9 × 54 = 486 metros.
hintsEs: Halla primero un décimo de 540.
Multiplica ese décimo por 9.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.2) The Tokyo building will be 6/5 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
onLevel.explanation: You need 6/5 of 540. One fifth of 540 is 108. Six fifths is 6 × 108 = 648 meters. That is taller than 540, because 6/5 is greater than 1.
choiceFeedback: 108 meters is only 1/5 of 540 — you still need 6 of those fifths.
432 meters SUBTRACTS a fifth (540 − 108) instead of taking 6 fifths.
450 meters is 5/6 of 540 — that flips the fraction, and it belongs to the London building.
hints: First find one fifth of 540.
6/5 means six of those fifths — will that be more or less than 540?
onLevel.stemEs: El edificio de Tokio será 6/5 de alto que el One World Trade Center (540 metros). ¿Qué altura tendrá?
onLevel.explanationEs: Necesitas 6/5 de 540. Un quinto de 540 es 108. Seis quintos son 6 × 108 = 648 metros. Es más alto que 540, porque 6/5 es mayor que 1.
hintsEs: Halla primero un quinto de 540.
6/5 significa seis de esos quintos — ¿eso será más o menos que 540?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.3) The 50 rides take 625 minutes. About how many HOURS is that?
onLevel.explanation: 625 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.42, so it would take about 10.42 hours to transport 4,000 passengers.
choiceFeedback: 6.25 moves the decimal two places — that divides by 100, but an hour is 60 minutes.
12.5 is the minutes for ONE ride, not the hours for all 50.
62.5 divides by 10 — an hour is 60 minutes, not 10.
hints: How many minutes are in one hour?
Divide the total minutes by 60.
onLevel.stemEs: Los 50 viajes toman 625 minutos. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas HORAS son?
onLevel.explanationEs: 625 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.42, así que tomaría unas 10.42 horas transportar a 4,000 pasajeros.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos minutos tiene una hora?
Divide los minutos totales entre 60.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.3) How does the answer change for 2,000 passengers? Each ride carries 80 passengers and takes 12.5 minutes. How many MINUTES are needed?
onLevel.explanation: 2,000 ÷ 80 = 25 rides, and 25 × 12.5 = 312.5 minutes — half the passengers, half the 625 minutes.
choiceFeedback: 31.25 shifts the decimal one place left — 25 × 12.5 is more than 25 × 10 = 250.
300 uses 12 minutes per ride instead of 12.5 — the missing 0.5 costs 12.5 minutes across 25 rides.
3,125 shifts the decimal one place right — check with estimation: 25 × 12.5 is close to 25 × 12 = 300.
hints: First find the rides: 2,000 ÷ 80.
That is 25 rides at 12.5 minutes each.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cómo cambia la respuesta para 2,000 pasajeros? Cada viaje lleva 80 pasajeros y toma 12.5 minutos. ¿Cuántos MINUTOS se necesitan?
onLevel.explanationEs: 2,000 ÷ 80 = 25 viajes, y 25 × 12.5 = 312.5 minutos — la mitad de los pasajeros, la mitad de los 625 minutos.
hintsEs: Halla primero los viajes: 2,000 ÷ 80.
Eso son 25 viajes de 12.5 minutos cada uno.

workedExample.work: (Lesson 1.3) Apply — What Time Is It? The new year starts at midnight on January 1st. What time will it be 2,022 minutes after midnight?
workedExample.workEs: Aplica — ¿Qué hora es? El año nuevo empieza a la medianoche del 1 de enero. ¿Qué hora será 2,022 minutos después de la medianoche?

workedExample.label: A classmate at our table answered
workedExample.labelEs: Un compañero de nuestra mesa respondió

onLevel.correctWork: The correct answer is 9:42 a.m. on January 2. 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 remainder 42, so 2,022 minutes is 33 hours 42 minutes. That is 24 hours (one full day) plus 9 hours 42 minutes — 9:42 a.m. on January 2.
onLevel.correctWorkEs: La respuesta correcta es 9:42 a. m. del 2 de enero. 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 con residuo 42, así que 2,022 minutos son 33 horas y 42 minutos. Eso es 24 horas (un día completo) más 9 horas y 42 minutos — 9:42 a. m. del 2 de enero.
hints: Divide 2,022 by 60 to get hours and leftover minutes.
hintsEs: Divide 2,022 entre 60 para obtener horas y minutos sobrantes.

extending.stem: (Lesson 1.3) Apply — What Time Is It? The new year starts at midnight on January 1st. What time will it be 2,022 minutes after midnight?
extending.explanation: 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 remainder 42, so 2,022 minutes is 33 hours 42 minutes. That is 24 hours (one full day) plus 9 hours 42 minutes — 9:42 a.m. on January 2.
choiceFeedback: That reads 2,022 minutes as 20 hours 22 minutes — but minutes must be DIVIDED by 60, not split by place value.
33 hours is more than one full day, so the clock has rolled past midnight into January 2.
After subtracting the 24-hour day, 9 hours 42 minutes past midnight is morning, not evening.

33 hours is one full day plus how many hours?

optional.instructions: (Lesson 1.1) Sort each thought: does it help a doer of math, or keep a thinker stuck?
optional.instructionsEs: Clasifica cada pensamiento: ¿ayuda a un hacedor de matemáticas o mantiene atascado al pensador?
optional.label: Sort each thought by the kind of thinking it shows.
optional.labelEs: Clasifica cada pensamiento según el tipo de razonamiento que muestra.

categories.label: Doer-of-math thinking
items: Let me look for a different entry point.
An estimate first will help me check my answer.
itemsEs: Todavía no puedo hacer esto... todavía.
Los errores le dan información a mi cerebro.
Voy a buscar otro punto de entrada.
Estimar primero me ayudará a comprobar mi respuesta.

categories.label: Stuck thinking
items: I'm just not a math person.
If it's hard, I should quit.
There is only one right way to solve it.
Being fast is the same as being smart.
itemsEs: Simplemente no soy una persona de matemáticas.
Solo hay una forma correcta de resolverlo.
Ser rápido es lo mismo que ser inteligente.

hints: Doer-of-math thoughts leave a next step open: try, estimate, look again.
Stuck thoughts close the door: quit, never, only one way.
hintsEs: Los pensamientos de hacedor dejan abierto un siguiente paso: intentar, estimar, mirar de nuevo.
Los pensamientos atascados cierran la puerta: rendirse, nunca, una sola forma.
optional.explanation: Doer-of-math thoughts keep the problem open — 'yet', 'a different entry point', and 'estimate first' all name a next move. Stuck thoughts end the work before it starts: 'not a math person', 'quit', 'only one way', and 'fast means smart' are all claims this lesson pushes back on.
optional.explanationEs: Los pensamientos de hacedor mantienen el problema abierto: 'todavía', 'otro punto de entrada' y 'estimar primero' nombran un siguiente paso. Los pensamientos atascados terminan el trabajo antes de empezar: 'no soy de matemáticas', 'rendirse', 'una sola forma' y 'rápido es inteligente' son ideas que esta lección refuta.

practice.commonMistake: Converting minutes to hours by moving the decimal point — 625 minutes is NOT 6.25 hours. An hour is 60 minutes, so divide by 60: 625 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.42 hours.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 1.2) Which statement best shows what this lesson means by "math is exploring and thinking"?
choices: We compute as fast as possible and move on to the next problem
We make sense of problems, plan a strategy, check our progress, and try other strategies at dead ends
We wait for someone to show us the one correct method
We only check our work when the answer looks wrong
exitTicket.explanation: The summary names a whole cycle, not one step. First make sense of the problem. Then develop a plan and check your progress as you go. Finally make sense of the solution in context.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It describes a cycle, not a single step.
Which option includes making sense, planning, AND checking?
exitTicket.stemEs: (Repaso rápido, de la lección 1.2) ¿Qué afirmación muestra mejor lo que esta lección quiere decir con «las matemáticas son explorar y pensar»?
choicesEs: Calculamos lo más rápido posible y pasamos al siguiente problema
Entendemos los problemas, planeamos una estrategia, revisamos nuestro avance y probamos otras estrategias cuando nos atoramos
Esperamos a que alguien nos muestre el único método correcto
Solo revisamos nuestro trabajo cuando la respuesta se ve mal
exitTicket.explanationEs: El resumen nombra un ciclo completo, no un solo paso. Primero entiende el problema. Luego desarrolla un plan y revisa tu avance mientras trabajas. Por último, dale sentido a la solución en su contexto.
hintsEs: Vuelve a mirar la diapositiva de resumen.
Describe un ciclo, no un solo paso.
¿Qué opción incluye entender, planear y revisar?

choiceFeedback: That is a quarter of 60, not half — try splitting 60 into 2 equal parts instead of 3.
That is a third of 60, not half — half means splitting into 2 equal parts.
That doubles 60 instead of splitting it into two equal parts.
choiceFeedbackEs: Eso es un cuarto de 60, no la mitad — divide 60 en 2 partes iguales, no en 3.
Eso es un tercio de 60, no la mitad — la mitad divide en 2 partes iguales.
Eso duplica 60 en vez de dividirlo en dos partes iguales.

choiceFeedback: That treats a quarter as one whole part out of one, not one part out of four equal parts.
That is four times too big — a quarter is one of four equal parts, not four times the number.
That multiplies by 4 instead of splitting into 4 equal parts.
choiceFeedbackEs: Eso trata un cuarto como una parte entera de uno, no una de cuatro partes iguales.
Eso es cuatro veces más grande — un cuarto es una de cuatro partes iguales, no cuatro veces el número.
Eso multiplica por 4 en vez de dividir en 4 partes iguales.

questions.stem: You multiply a whole number by a fraction smaller than 1. The answer is:
choices: Smaller than the number you started with
Bigger than the number you started with
questions.explanation: Taking a part of an amount leaves less than the whole amount, so the answer is smaller.
questions.stemEs: Multiplicas un número entero por una fracción menor que 1. La respuesta es:
choicesEs: Menor que el número con el que empezaste
Mayor que el número con el que empezaste
questions.explanationEs: Tomar una parte de una cantidad deja menos que la cantidad entera, así que la respuesta es menor.
choiceFeedback: Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a number smaller, not bigger.
A fraction less than 1 changes the size of the number — it doesn't leave it unchanged.
Multiplying by a fraction smaller than 1 still gives a nonzero part of the number, not zero.
choiceFeedbackEs: Multiplicar por una fracción menor que 1 hace el número más pequeño, no más grande.
Una fracción menor que 1 cambia el tamaño del número — no lo deja igual.
Multiplicar por una fracción menor que 1 sigue dando una parte del número, no cero.
